passage:
Dear Lipika,
I'm writing this instead of just putting a mark, because I want you to see what I saw.
In June your essays were four lines long, with no full stops. Your essay this week, about the flooded road outside your house, is fourteen lines. You used paragraphs. You wrote 'the water was the colour of tea', and that made me stop and read it twice. You spelt 'neighbour' right every single time.
I know the marks still aren't where you want them. But you are getting better, and I can point to exactly where.
Next task, and it's a stretch: write the same flood from your neighbour's point of view. Twelve lines, one describing word in each. I think you can do it. If you get stuck halfway, come and find me at lunch.
Deepa Ma'am

qa.q: How long were Lipika's essays in June?
qa.a: Four lines long, with no full stops.

qa.q: Why does Deepa Ma'am list such specific details instead of just writing 'good'?
qa.a: She wants Lipika to see real proof of progress, believing that visible improvement will bring back Lipika's wish to try.

qa.q: What choice about the next task makes it helpful, and why?
qa.a: Making it a stretch but doable, the same flood from the neighbour's view in twelve lines with a describing word in each, plus help at lunch; it builds on what Lipika can already do.

qa.q: How might Lipika feel reading 'the water was the colour of tea' quoted back?
qa.a: Lipika would probably feel surprised and proud that Lipika's own line made a teacher stop and read twice, and might start to believe that Lipika can write. 😊

grounding: A teacher points out specific improvements in a struggling student's writing and sets a next task that is hard but doable.

passage:
You want to know what worked with Anand, Elizabeth? Not a pep talk. He'd heard plenty of those.
He was failing chemistry, Class 10, sitting at the back with his hood up. First thing I did was go through his last five worksheets with a highlighter. Not for mistakes. For what he'd got right. Turned out he'd balanced every equation with two elements correctly. Every one. It was only the three-element ones that fell apart.
So I showed him. 'Look, Anand. Two elements, ten out of ten.' He actually leaned in. 'Okay, Salma Ma'am,' he said. 'Then what?'
Then I gave him one three-element equation, just one, with the first step done. He got it. Next day, two, no first step.
By March he was at 61. Not a miracle. But he stopped wearing the hood in class. I think that's when he started believing it.

qa.q: Which equations had Anand been balancing correctly?
qa.a: Every equation with two elements.

qa.q: What does Anand leaning in suggest about how he felt when Salma showed him the ten out of ten?
qa.a: It suggests surprise and a spark of hope; seeing proof that he could do part of it made trying seem worthwhile again.

qa.q: What choice did Salma make about the next tasks, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set one three-element equation with the first step done, then two without; each step was hard but doable, so Anand kept succeeding and building up.

qa.q: How might Anand have seen chemistry class before Salma's highlighter?
qa.a: He probably saw it as a place where he failed, hiding under his hood at the back with no sign that he got anything right.

grounding: A teacher shows a struggling student exactly what he already does well and sets the next task just beyond it, rebuilding his wish to try.

Pankaj, you asked how I got back into coding after I bombed the placement test. Honestly, I didn't plan a comeback. I planned one tiny problem a day.
After that test, I didn't open my laptop for three weeks. I'd convinced myself I just wasn't a coder. Then my sister said, 'Do one easy one, Hrithik. Just one.' Reverse a string. Took me forty minutes. Embarrassing.
But I wrote it in a notebook: Day 1, reverse a string. Day 2, count vowels. Day 3, find the largest number in a list.
By Day 30 the list filled two pages. Some days I'd just flip through it. It was proof, you know? Not a feeling. Proof.
Now I'm on Day 142, doing graph problems. I still fail sometimes. But I open the notebook, see page one, and think, okay, that guy couldn't reverse a string.

qa.q: What was the first problem Hrithik wrote in the notebook?
qa.a: Reverse a string, which took forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did the growing list matter so much to Hrithik?
qa.a: After the test Hrithik no longer trusted feelings about ability; the list was 'proof, not a feeling', clear evidence of getting better.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Hrithik, and why did it work?
qa.a: The sister's 'Do one easy one. Just one'; a task small enough to finish restarted the habit, and writing each one down built evidence that motivated the next.

qa.q: How might Pankaj, still nervous about coding, hear this story?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel encouraged that even someone who bombed a test and took forty minutes on a string recovered, and might start a one-problem-a-day list too.

grounding: A student who lost confidence in coding solves one tiny problem a day and records it, and the growing list becomes proof that drives the next step.

I'm Aparna, Rukmini's roommate in the girls' hostel. After Rukmini failed the data structures exam in December, she didn't touch her laptop for a while. She'd say 'I'm not a coding person' and change the topic.
In January the sticky notes started. Every night she solved one small problem, the kind first-years do, and wrote it on a yellow note above her desk: 'Jan 4, sum of digits.' 'Jan 5, palindrome check.' Some nights it took her an hour. Once she threw a pen.
By March the notes covered half the wall. I'd catch her standing in front of them before bed, just looking.
Last week she solved a linked list problem and moved on to green notes. I don't know exactly what has changed in her head. But she hasn't said 'not a coding person' in weeks.

qa.a: Aparna has gone from hearing 'I'm not a coding person' to seeing a wall of notes and a move to harder problems, and seems quietly impressed, though unsure what is happening inside.

subtype: Stuck in a job that stopped stretching [Actor]

Supervisor's note, university library, periodicals section. Tanuja.
Anushree (25) has been with us three years. Her work is accurate and on time. Nothing is wrong. But this month I noticed she sighs at the returns trolley, eats lunch alone at her desk scrolling, and on Tuesday she said to me, 'I could do this job asleep. Some days I think I am.'
She isn't unhappy with anyone. She seems flat, like a radio turned down.
I remembered that she once built a small spreadsheet to track damaged journals, unasked, and it was good.
Next step: I've offered her the lead on digitising the old maps collection. It needs new software and a short training course, which the library will pay for. She asked three questions in the first minute. I'll check in with her in four weeks.

qa.q: What did Anushree say to Tanuja on Tuesday?
qa.a: 'I could do this job asleep. Some days I think I am.'

qa.q: Why might Anushree feel flat even though nothing is wrong?
qa.a: Her work no longer stretches her; after three years of doing it well there is nothing new to grow into, so her energy has dropped.

qa.q: What choice did Tanuja make, and why is it likely to help?
qa.a: Offering Anushree the lead on digitising the maps, with new software and a paid course; a real challenge that grows her skill could bring back her energy, as her three quick questions suggest.

qa.q: How might Anushree's flatness look to the rest of the library team?
qa.a: They might not notice, since her work is accurate, or might think she is simply quiet; only a watchful supervisor sees the radio turned down.

grounding: A supervisor notices a capable young employee feeling flat in a routine job with nothing wrong, and offers a new project to stretch her.

subtype: Stuck in a job that stopped stretching [Actor]

Sunday night
Another week of the same forty test cases. Pass, pass, pass. Good pay, nice team, a manager who says thank you. And I feel like old rice. Nothing's wrong, which is the annoying part. What am I even complaining about?
Chetan came over for chai and I said it out loud for the first time. He didn't tell me to be grateful. He said, 'Saurabh, when did you last learn something at work?' I actually couldn't remember. Maybe eighteen months ago.
He's doing an evening course in embedded systems and made me look at the syllabus. Something woke up in my chest reading it. Microcontrollers! I used to love that stuff in college.
Signed up. Starts Tuesday. First time in months I'm looking forward to a weekday.

qa.q: What course is Chetan doing?
qa.a: An evening course in embedded systems.

qa.q: Why does Saurabh find the flatness 'annoying'?
qa.a: Nothing is actually wrong, good pay, a nice team, so Saurabh feels there's no right to complain, yet still feels like 'old rice'; having no clear reason makes it confusing.

qa.a: 'When did you last learn something at work?'; it pointed to the missing challenge rather than telling Saurabh to be grateful, and led to signing up for the course.

qa.a: Chetan takes it seriously instead of dismissing it, seeming to recognise the feeling of being under-stretched and wanting Saurabh to find that spark again.

passage:
Neelam had never cared about science. Plants, pulleys, whatever. But this term Swati had pulled her into the Sunflower Group with three other girls, and the group had a model of the water cycle due on Friday.
On Thursday evening the power went out in their whole colony. The glue gun died halfway through the clouds.
Neelam could have gone home. Instead she ran to her house for candles and a tube of craft glue, and stayed till nine, cutting cotton-wool clouds by candlelight while Swati read out the steps.
'You don't even like science,' Swati said, laughing.
'I like us,' Neelam said, and pressed the last cloud into place.
Years later Neelam would still remember the smell of wax and wet cotton, and the five of them lifting the model onto the teacher's table together.

qa.q: What did the Sunflower Group have to make?
qa.a: A model of the water cycle, due on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Neelam stay till nine when she didn't care about science?
qa.a: The group mattered to her; being part of 'us' with Swati and the others made the work worth doing, power cut or not.

qa.q: What choice showed belonging at work, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Running home for candles and glue instead of leaving; the group finished the model and carried it up together on Friday.

qa.q: How might Swati feel hearing 'I like us'?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel warm and pleased, knowing that pulling Neelam into the group made her feel she belonged.

grounding: A child who does not care about the subject works hard on a group model through a power cut because the group matters to her.

subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage:
Rekha had done Kathak since she was six, every Tuesday and Friday at the dance school above the sweet shop in Lucknow. Then, in Class 9, she moved into Charu's group. Charu's group went to the mall after school, knew all the new songs and called classical dance 'so aunty'.
When Charu saw the ghungroo in Rekha's bag, she laughed. 'You still do that? Cute.'
The next week Rekha told her guru she had too much homework. She put the ghungroo in the steel trunk under her bed.
For months it felt fine. Mall, songs, Charu's jokes.
Then in December, walking past the sweet shop, she heard the tabla upstairs and the tatkar of small feet. She stood on the pavement until the piece ended, her chest aching, and couldn't explain to Charu why she had gone so quiet.

qa.q: Where did Rekha put her ghungroo?
qa.a: In the steel trunk under her bed.

qa.q: Why did Rekha give up Kathak after Charu's laugh?
qa.a: Belonging to Charu's group mattered so much that looking 'aunty' felt like a risk; giving up dance seemed a small price to fit in.

qa.q: What was the turning point in December, and what could Rekha choose now?
qa.a: Hearing the tabla above the sweet shop and feeling her chest ache; Rekha could return to class, even one day a week, and decide what she loves without waiting for Charu's verdict.

qa.q: How might Charu see Rekha's sudden quietness on the pavement?
qa.a: Charu probably has no idea why; her 'Cute' was a throwaway laugh, and she may not realise it cost Rekha something she loved.

grounding: A teenager quits a much-loved dance class because her new group finds it uncool, and feels the loss months later.

Ujjwal, you've been made team lead and you've printed a poster that says 'Excellence Every Day'. Sit. Let me tell you about the depot.

The cyclone warning came at 6 p.m. The night shift at the customer helpline in Visakhapatnam was half empty, and calls were flooding in about cancelled trains. Head office sent a message: 'Stay strong, team! Customer first!'

qa.a: Lalremsiami would likely feel proud of helping, since one simple question turned Damini's big wish into something she could do every day. 🙂

passage:
I'm Vikas, Sunaina's younger brother. Sunaina is going to be a doctor. Everyone in our building knows, because she tells them. The toy stethoscope she got at six still hangs on her cupboard, and there's a poster of the human heart above her bed.
But here's what I see. Her biology notebook has been at the bottom of her bag since the holidays. When Papa asked which exam she needs to take, she said, 'The medical one,' and changed the subject. In the evenings she watches hospital shows and says, 'That'll be me.'
Last week her friend Gayatri asked what she was doing this month to get there. Sunaina went quiet for a long time.
I don't know what she was thinking. Maybe she was scared. Maybe she'd just never thought about it. Afterwards, though, she took out the biology notebook.

qa.q: What hangs on Sunaina's cupboard?
qa.a: The toy stethoscope she got at six.

qa.q: What might Sunaina's long silence after Gayatri's question suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she realised she had no plan for the month; the dream was vivid, but the near steps were missing, and that may have worried her.

qa.q: What choice after Gayatri's question could start to close the gap, and why?
qa.a: Taking out the biology notebook; one concrete step this month, like a weekly biology target, links the far goal to everyday action.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the gap between Sunaina's dream and her days?
qa.a: Vikas notices the posters and the talk but also the buried notebook and vague answers, and is unsure whether she is scared or has simply never thought about the steps.

grounding: A younger brother observes a teenager who talks constantly about becoming a doctor but has no near-term plan, until a friend's question stops her.
